lesson.title: Why Wires Aren't Free: Resistance in Ordinary Conductors
lesson.summary: Even a plain length of copper wire has measurable resistance, governed by its material, length, and thickness, which is why long or thin wire runs waste real power and drop real voltage.
lesson.body:
Every resistor discussed so far has been a discrete component, a part chosen specifically to add opposition to current. But resistance is not a special property limited to those parts. Any real conductor, including the plain wire connecting a battery to a load, is made of imperfect material, not the zero resistance ideal wire assumed in simple circuit diagrams. That real resistance follows the same physics as any resistor and can be calculated directly from the wire's dimensions.

The governing formula is R = rho times L divided by A, where rho, the resistivity, is a property of the material itself, measured in ohm meters, L is the length of the wire, and A is its cross sectional area. Copper, the most common wire material, has a resistivity of about 1.68 times 10 to the negative 8 ohm meters at room temperature. The formula makes physical sense on inspection: a longer wire forces electrons through more collisions with the material's atomic lattice, raising resistance in direct proportion to length, while a thicker wire gives electrons more parallel cross sectional room to flow through, lowering resistance in inverse proportion to area.

Worked example: take 10 meters of copper wire with a diameter of 1 millimeter, so a radius of 0.5 millimeters, or 0.0005 meters. The cross sectional area is A = pi times radius squared = pi times 0.0005 squared = pi times 0.00000025, which comes out to about 7.854e-7 square meters. Now R = rho times L divided by A = 1.68e-8 times 10, divided by 7.854e-7. The numerator is 1.68e-7, and dividing by 7.854e-7 gives approximately 0.214 ohms. Ten meters of ordinary 1 millimeter copper wire, then, carries about a fifth of an ohm of resistance, small, but not zero.

That small number matters more than it looks. If this wire carries 10 amps, the power wasted as heat is I squared times R = 100 times 0.214, about 21.4 watts, dissipated along the wire itself rather than delivered to the load, and the voltage drop along the wire is V = IR = 10 times 0.214 = 2.14 volts, a meaningful loss if the source supplies only 12 volts. This is exactly why long extension cords, battery cables, and circuit board traces are specified with a minimum wire gauge for a given current, thin wire over a long run is a real resistor whether anyone intended it to be one or not.

One more wrinkle worth knowing: resistivity itself rises with temperature for metals like copper, so a wire carrying heavy current and warming up has measurably higher resistance than the same wire cold, which is part of why fuses and wire gauge tables build in margin. Treating connecting wire as ideal, zero resistance conductor is a fine approximation for short, thick runs at modest current, but it is always an approximation, not a law of physics.

Standard wire gauge tables exist specifically to turn this formula into a quick lookup, listing the resistance per unit length for each standard wire diameter so an engineer does not have to compute pi times radius squared by hand every time. A thicker gauge, meaning a lower gauge number in the common American Wire Gauge system, always buys lower resistance per meter at the cost of more copper, more weight, and more expense, which is the practical tradeoff behind choosing wire size for any given current and acceptable voltage drop.
